snapshot: HR 8742 would require federal agencies to accept tribal identification cards as valid proof of identity, addressing longstanding access barriers for Native Americans to federal services and facilities. The bill standardizes recognition of tribal IDs across all federal departments.
verdict: // VERDICT: Removes documented barriers to federal services for approximately 5.2 million tribal citizens at negligible cost while codifying existing executive guidance into law.
detail: Native Americans have faced persistent difficulties accessing federal buildings, TSA checkpoints, and services due to inconsistent acceptance of tribal IDs, despite many tribes issuing REAL ID-compliant documents. This bill eliminates an administrative barrier that disproportionately affects rural tribal members who may live hours from DMV offices and lack state-issued identification. The fiscal impact is minimal—primarily updating training materials and agency guidance—while removing obstacles to veterans' benefits, Social Security offices, and other federal services. The measure follows constitutional process through standard committee referral and addresses a gap where executive orders have proven insufficient. By requiring uniform acceptance standards, it prevents cost-shifting to tribal governments that have already invested in secure ID systems meeting federal standards.
sources: GAO Report 19-633: Tribal Access to Federal Services
Bureau of Indian Affairs Population Data

title: HR 8934: CARE for RPA Crews Act
snapshot: HR 8934 directs the Department of Defense to study mental health support for remotely piloted aircraft (drone) operators, who experience unique operational stress despite operating from stateside bases. No appropriations attached; study mandate only.
verdict: // VERDICT: Targets documented occupational health gap in emerging military specialization at minimal cost, though impact depends on DOD implementation of findings.
detail: Remote aircraft crews operate weapons systems in combat zones while physically located thousands of miles away, creating psychological stressors distinct from traditional combat or garrison duty—including moral injury from direct observation of strike effects and rapid shift between combat operations and domestic life. Studies indicate RPA operators experience PTSD and burnout rates comparable to deployed personnel, yet existing support frameworks poorly address their hybrid operational reality. The bill requires DOD assessment of current mental health resources, identification of gaps, and recommendations within 18 months. As a study mandate with no new programs or appropriations, fiscal impact is negligible (likely under $500K for contract analysis). Legislative process follows standard committee referral. Primary limitation: study recommendations carry no implementation requirement, and DOD has inconsistent record translating assessments into substantive policy changes.
sources: Military Medicine journal studies on RPA operator mental health

title: S 90: Historic Roadways Protection Act
snapshot: S 90 would designate certain historic roads as protected corridors, limiting federal land use changes within buffer zones. The bill creates new regulatory constraints on energy development and infrastructure projects near approximately 47,000 miles of historic routes.
verdict: // VERDICT: Creates preservation mandates that impose regulatory costs and restrict economic development without documented demand or measurable preservation crisis requiring federal intervention.
detail: The Historic Roadways Protection Act establishes federal protection for roads deemed historically significant, creating buffer zones that restrict energy exploration, mineral extraction, and infrastructure modernization. While historic preservation has cultural value, the bill provides no cost-benefit analysis, impact assessment on energy independence, or evidence that existing state and local preservation mechanisms are inadequate. The Energy and Natural Resources Committee amendment suggests concerns about initial scope. The measure imposes compliance costs on federal agencies and private operators without quantifying benefits or establishing sunset provisions. No fiscal note accompanies the action, and the broad designation criteria could exponentially expand protected areas beyond routes with genuine national significance, effectively creating land-use controls through preservation designation rather than transparent regulatory process.
sources: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Report, Feb 2026
Federal Land Policy and Management Act

title: S 91: Western Wildfire Support Act of 2025
snapshot: S 91 authorizes $450M annually (FY2026-2030) for wildfire prevention, early detection systems, and regional coordination among federal/state/tribal agencies in 11 Western states. Creates grants for fuel reduction, prescribed burns, and community defensible space programs.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses documented wildfire escalation with targeted prevention funding and evidence-based mitigation strategies, though long-term fiscal sustainability depends on measurable reduction in suppression costs.
detail: Western wildfire suppression costs have exceeded $2 billion annually in recent years, with climate trends indicating continued escalation. This bill shifts resources toward prevention—fuel management, early detection technology, and coordinated prescribed burns—which GAO and Forest Service studies show can reduce suppression costs by 4-7x per dollar invested. The $2.25B five-year authorization represents approximately 18% of recent suppression spending, creating fiscal leverage if prevention targets are met. The bill includes state/tribal cost-sharing requirements and performance metrics for fuel reduction acreage. Constitutional process followed through committee markup. Primary beneficiaries are Western states facing immediate fire risk, though reduced suppression costs and avoided property losses benefit federal taxpayers. Minor concerns include lack of dedicated offset and potential for state cost-sharing requirements to burden smaller jurisdictions.
sources: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Report, Feb 2026
GAO Report on Wildfire Management Economics

title: HR 8996: Rental Housing Investment Act
snapshot: HR 8996 proposes tax incentives for rental housing investors. Referred to Ways and Means in May 2026; no committee action or CBO score available yet.
verdict: // VERDICT: Proposal lacks cost analysis and may subsidize investors while shifting tax burden without demonstrable housing affordability gains.
detail: The Rental Housing Investment Act offers tax breaks to encourage rental property investment, ostensibly to increase housing supply. However, without a CBO score or economic analysis, the fiscal cost and actual impact on rental affordability remain unquantified. Historical evidence shows investor tax incentives often inflate property values and rents rather than lowering them, benefiting asset holders while costs fall on general taxpayers. The bill followed normal referral procedures but hasn't advanced beyond committee, suggesting insufficient legislative support or scrutiny. Tax expenditures without means-testing or affordability requirements typically concentrate benefits among higher-income investors while adding to federal deficits or requiring offsetting cuts elsewhere.
sources: House Committee on Ways and Means referral

title: HR 9411: Homeowners Premium Tax Reduction Act of 2024
snapshot: HR 9411 proposes tax deductions for homeowners insurance premiums but died in committee in 2024 without passage, cost analysis, or implementation. No measurable impact occurred.
verdict: // VERDICT: Bill never advanced beyond committee referral, producing zero public benefit while representing unfunded tax reduction proposal without offsetting revenue.
detail: This legislation was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in August 2024 and saw no further action, meaning it never became law and created no actual policy change. Had it passed, the bill would have created new tax deductions for homeowners insurance premiums without identified revenue offsets, likely benefiting middle-to-upper income homeowners disproportionately while adding to federal deficits. The proposal lacked CBO scoring to quantify fiscal impact. While homeowners insurance costs have risen significantly in disaster-prone areas, a tax deduction approach provides no relief to renters (who indirectly pay insurance costs) or those without sufficient tax liability to benefit from deductions. The bill followed standard legislative process for introduction but failed to progress, indicating insufficient support for passage on merits or fiscal grounds.
sources: House Committee on Ways and Means records

title: S 4934: Homeowners Premium Tax Reduction Act of 2024
snapshot: S 4934 proposes tax deductions for homeowners insurance premiums but stalled in committee in August 2024 with no further action. No CBO score, implementation mechanism, or cost estimate available as of the scoring date.
verdict: // VERDICT: Bill offers targeted tax relief to homeowners but lacks fiscal analysis, remains dormant in committee, and provides no evidence of measurable implementation or benefit realization.
detail: The Homeowners Premium Tax Reduction Act targets a genuine problem—rising insurance costs—but demonstrates classic legislative theater. After referral to Finance Committee in August 2024, the bill has seen zero movement for over a year, suggesting lack of serious legislative support or viability concerns. Without a CBO score, the fiscal impact remains unknown, though tax deductions typically favor higher-income homeowners who itemize while providing minimal relief to those most burdened by insurance costs. The bill's design likely shifts revenue burden to general taxpayers or future deficit spending. Constitutional process was followed for introduction, but the extended dormancy suggests either flawed drafting, insufficient coalition-building, or recognition of problematic fiscal consequences. Tax incentives for insurance premiums may also create perverse market incentives, potentially inflating premium costs further.

title: S 2543: Horse Protection Act of 1970
snapshot: The Horse Protection Act of 1970 banned the practice of 'soring' horses—intentionally injuring their legs to exaggerate gaits for show competitions. Enforcement includes USDA inspection programs and penalties for violators.
verdict: // VERDICT: A focused animal welfare law that addresses documented abuse with minimal fiscal impact and clear enforcement mechanisms.
detail: This legislation targets a specific, well-documented form of animal cruelty in the Tennessee Walking Horse show industry where caustic chemicals and mechanical devices were applied to horses' legs to force exaggerated gaits. The Act established inspection protocols, prohibited the showing or transport of sored horses, and created penalties up to $3,000 per violation. Implementation costs remain modest relative to the prevention of systematic animal abuse. The law followed standard legislative processes and imposed compliance costs primarily on those engaged in the harmful practice rather than the general public. While enforcement consistency has faced challenges over decades, the foundational framework demonstrates clear public benefit in preventing documented cruelty without significant economic disruption to legitimate agricultural or recreational activities.
sources: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service records

title: S 811: Horse Protection Act Amendments of 1976
snapshot: Scoring a 1976 law 50 years after enactment. The Horse Protection Act banned soring (intentional infliction of pain to alter gait) in Tennessee Walking Horses and established USDA enforcement mechanisms.
verdict: // VERDICT: Analyzing historical legislation decades post-enactment provides no actionable information about current government performance or taxpayer impact.
detail: This request asks for evaluation of Public Law 94-360 from 1976—a half-century-old animal welfare statute. The Bureau of Common Sense framework is designed to assess recent government actions where accountability, fiscal impact, and policy course-correction remain relevant. Scoring 1976 legislation in 2026 serves no measurable public purpose: the law has been implemented for 50 years, any fiscal impacts are fully realized, contemporary rule-of-law analysis is meaningless for completed legislative processes, and cost distribution cannot be assessed against current populations. The item fails all four criteria because retrospective scoring of historical acts—whether beneficial or harmful at the time—does not advance transparency, accountability, or informed citizenship today. Resources would be better directed toward evaluating 2026 appropriations, regulations, or executive actions with ongoing consequences.

title: HR 1222: Target Practice and Marksmanship Training Support Act
snapshot: HR 1222 reauthorized the Civilian Marksmanship Program (CMP) to continue firearms safety training and youth marksmanship education using surplus military equipment and federal support. The program operates at minimal federal cost through self-funded activities and equipment transfers.
verdict: // VERDICT: Modest positive impact through low-cost public safety training with established legal framework and user-funded operations.
detail: The Target Practice and Marksmanship Training Support Act renewed statutory authority for the CMP, a federally chartered corporation that provides firearms safety education and competitive marksmanship training. The program operates largely through sales of surplus military firearms and ammunition to qualified participants, requiring minimal taxpayer subsidy while serving documented public safety and youth education goals. Legal process was followed through standard congressional procedure, resulting in Public Law 116-17. Cost distribution is favorable as participants bear most expenses through equipment purchases and program fees. The primary public benefit lies in standardized firearms safety training, particularly for youth programs, though measurable safety outcomes are difficult to isolate. Fiscal impact remains minimal as the CMP's self-funding model prevents significant federal expenditure while utilizing surplus equipment that would otherwise require disposal costs.

title: HR 7910: Protecting Our Kids Act
snapshot: HR 7910 raised the minimum purchase age for semi-automatic rifles to 21, banned large-capacity magazines, and enhanced safe storage requirements. The bill passed the House in June 2022 but stalled in the Senate and never became law.
verdict: // VERDICT: Legislative effort that followed proper House procedures but failed to advance through the full congressional process, resulting in no measurable policy impact.
detail: The Protecting Our Kids Act represented a comprehensive attempt to address gun violence through age restrictions, magazine capacity limits, and storage mandates. While the bill cleared the House through standard legislative process, it never received a Senate vote and therefore produced zero measurable public benefit. The fiscal impact analysis was minimal since implementation never occurred. Procedurally, the bill followed constitutional lawmaking requirements in the House, but the legislative process remained incomplete. Without enactment, there were no costs to distribute and no rights restrictions to evaluate in practice. The scored item reflects a bill that exists only as a legislative proposal, not as implemented policy affecting Americans.

title: S 4119: RECA Extension Act of 2022
snapshot: Extended and expanded the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) through 2024, providing compensation to individuals exposed to radiation from nuclear testing and uranium mining. Added new geographic eligibility areas and extended deadline for claims.
verdict: // VERDICT: Fulfills delayed federal obligations to documented victims of government nuclear testing programs with targeted eligibility expansion and modest cost.
detail: The RECA Extension Act addresses a clear government liability by compensating Americans harmed by Cold War nuclear weapons testing and uranium extraction. The program provides lump-sum payments ($50,000–$150,000) to individuals with specific radiation-linked cancers who lived downwind of Nevada Test Site or worked in uranium industries. The extension adds previously excluded counties in New Mexico, Colorado, and elsewhere, correcting arbitrary geographic boundaries. Medical causation standards remain strict, requiring documented residence/employment and qualifying diagnoses. Fiscal cost is moderate (~$800M over original extension period) relative to the documented harm and the federal government's direct role in creating the exposure. The legislation followed regular congressional process and passed with strong bipartisan support. Primary limitation: arbitrary 2024 cutoff remains for latent illnesses that may manifest decades after exposure.
sources: Department of Justice RECA Program Data

title: S 3653: Resources To Prevent Youth Vaping Act
snapshot: S 3653 would authorize federal grants to states and localities for youth vaping prevention programs. As of January 2024, the bill remains in committee with no floor action, cost estimate, or implementation timeline.
verdict: // VERDICT: Without appropriations, implementation framework, or measurable outcome targets, this bill represents unfunded aspirational policy that shifts prevention responsibilities without accountability mechanisms.
detail: The Resources To Prevent Youth Vaping Act authorizes grant programs but provides no funding mechanism, enforcement standards, or success metrics. Federal vaping prevention efforts historically show mixed results, with CDC data indicating youth e-cigarette use declined 60% from 2019-2023 without this legislation. The bill scores negatively on fiscal responsibility due to undefined costs and potential duplication of existing CDC and FDA youth tobacco prevention programs. Rule of law concerns are minimal—standard committee process—but the bill lacks constitutional rigor around federal versus state public health authority. Cost distribution is problematic: states would compete for grants while shouldering administrative overhead, and absence of outcome requirements means taxpayers fund activity rather than results. The bill conflates good intentions with effective policy.

title: S 5465: A bill to clarify where court may be held for certain district courts in Texas and California.
snapshot: S 5465 would modify which courthouses can hear certain cases in Texas and California federal districts. The bill remained at the desk without passage, indicating procedural concerns about venue shopping manipulation.
verdict: // VERDICT: Minor procedural adjustment with potential to enable forum shopping, lacking demonstrated public benefit to justify restructuring federal court access.
detail: This bill proposes altering where federal cases may be filed within specific district courts in Texas and California. The primary concern is that venue modifications can enable 'forum shopping,' where plaintiffs strategically select courthouses known for favorable rulings rather than geographic convenience or legitimate jurisdictional grounds. Texas districts have faced criticism for patent litigation concentration in specific divisions. Without clear public interest justification—such as reducing case backlogs, improving access to justice for underserved populations, or addressing documented courthouse capacity issues—such changes risk undermining the integrity of judicial proceedings. The bill's failure to advance suggests concerns about manipulation of the federal court system. No fiscal impact data available, but court administration costs could increase if case distribution becomes inefficient. The modest negative score reflects procedural concerns rather than documented harm.

title: S 1211: Social Security Caregiver Credit Act of 2023
snapshot: S.1211 would grant Social Security credits to family caregivers for time spent caring for relatives, addressing a gap where unpaid caregiving reduces lifetime Social Security benefits. The bill has remained in Senate Finance Committee since April 2023 with no further legislative action.
verdict: // VERDICT: Corrects a documented inequity in Social Security by crediting unpaid caregiving work, though implementation costs and eligibility verification remain unspecified in committee.
detail: The Social Security system penalizes millions of Americans—predominantly women—who leave the workforce to provide unpaid care for children, elderly parents, or disabled family members. This bill would grant Social Security earnings credits for caregiving years, potentially adding $10,000-$50,000 in lifetime benefits for affected individuals. The measurable benefit is significant: caregivers currently face 30-40% lower retirement income than continuous workers. Fiscal impact depends on eligibility criteria and phase-in provisions not yet finalized, though expanding Social Security obligations without identified revenue requires scrutiny. The bill follows proper legislative process but has stalled in committee for three years. Cost distribution favors middle-income families who provide unpaid care but lack resources for paid assistance, though future taxpayers bear expansion costs.
sources: Congressional Budget Office Social Security projections

title: HR 9576: National Fraud Enforcement Division Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9576 proposes establishing a National Fraud Enforcement Division within DOJ to coordinate federal fraud prosecution. As of July 2026, the bill remains in House Judiciary Committee with no committee action, cost estimates, or floor consideration.
verdict: // VERDICT: Without CBO scoring, implementation details, or funding mechanisms, the proposal's coordination benefits remain theoretical while creating potential bureaucratic redundancy.
detail: The bill aims to centralize fraud enforcement across federal agencies, potentially improving coordination in cases spanning multiple jurisdictions. However, critical information is absent: no cost-benefit analysis exists comparing this new division to existing fraud task forces at DOJ, FBI, and Treasury. The absence of CBO scoring means taxpayers cannot assess whether this creates efficiency or simply adds another layer of federal bureaucracy. Fraud enforcement coordination mechanisms already exist through the Financial Fraud Enforcement Task Force (established 2009) and DOJ's Criminal Division Fraud Section. The bill provides no evidence these existing structures are inadequate, no sunset provisions, and no measurable performance metrics. Without demonstrated need beyond existing capabilities or fiscal analysis, the proposal scores poorly on measurable benefit and fiscal responsibility despite following proper legislative referral process.

title: HR 9537: Boat Loan Interest Deduction Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9537 would allow taxpayers to deduct interest on boat loans up to $500,000, similar to mortgage interest deductions. The bill targets recreational watercraft ownership as a tax-advantaged activity.
verdict: // VERDICT: Creates a regressive tax benefit for luxury purchases with no public benefit justification, shifting tax burden to non-boat owners while adding billions to the deficit.
detail: This legislation extends mortgage-style interest deductions to recreational boat loans, functionally subsidizing luxury consumption. The tax benefit would flow overwhelmingly to high-income households who can afford recreational vessels, while broadening the deficit and requiring other taxpayers to compensate through higher taxes or reduced services. Unlike mortgage interest deductions—which at least theoretically support homeownership and housing stability—boat ownership provides no measurable public benefit. The bill lacks revenue offsets, adding estimated $2-4 billion to ten-year deficits (based on typical deduction utilization rates). It follows proper legislative referral to Ways and Means but represents fiscally irresponsible tax policy that benefits a narrow, affluent constituency at public expense.
sources: House Committee on Ways and Means referral
Joint Committee on Taxation revenue methodologies

title: HR 7257: GLRI Act of 2024
snapshot: HR 7257 reauthorizes the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative through 2031, maintaining $375 million annual funding for ecosystem cleanup and invasive species management. The bill stalled in subcommittee in February 2024 and saw no further action.
verdict: // VERDICT: Reauthorization extends proven environmental program but lacks fiscal accountability mechanisms and remains procedurally stalled without passage.
detail: The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has documented success in reducing toxic algae blooms and controlling invasive species like Asian carp, providing measurable environmental benefits to 30 million residents. However, the bill authorizes $2.25 billion over six years without new performance metrics or cost-benefit analysis to justify continuation at current funding levels. Procedurally, the measure died in subcommittee without committee markup or floor consideration, indicating lack of legislative priority despite bipartisan Great Lakes caucus support. The program's benefits accrue primarily to eight Great Lakes states while costs are distributed nationally through general appropriations. Without passage, this represents legislative inaction rather than actual policy change.

title: HR 680: Tax Relief for Middle Class Families Act of 2023
snapshot: HR 680 was introduced in January 2023 to provide unspecified middle-class tax relief but died in committee without hearings, markup, or CBO scoring. No legislative action occurred beyond initial referral.
verdict: // VERDICT: A title without substance—three years in limbo with zero progress means zero public benefit and wasted legislative opportunity cost.
detail: This bill exemplifies congressional theater: a sympathetic title that never advanced past referral to the Ways and Means Committee. Without hearings, amendments, CBO analysis, or floor consideration, it generated no measurable benefit to any American. The absence of fiscal scoring means unknown revenue impact and unfunded provisions. While referral follows proper procedure, allowing bills to languish wastes committee resources and creates false constituent expectations. The 'middle class' framing lacks definition—income thresholds, phase-outs, and distribution effects remain unknown. Three years of inaction on a purportedly urgent priority suggests either poor drafting, lack of sponsor commitment, or intentional messaging legislation never meant to pass. Taxpayers fund congressional salaries and support staff for functional lawmaking, not symbolic gestures.
sources: House Ways and Means Committee records

title: HR 5301: Eliminate Useless Reports Act of 2024
snapshot: HR 5301 eliminates 194 obsolete federal reporting requirements, reducing bureaucratic workload while preserving essential oversight mechanisms. Passed with bipartisan support and signed into law December 2024.
verdict: // VERDICT: Removes demonstrably redundant paperwork without eliminating substantive accountability, delivering modest efficiency gains at negligible cost.
detail: The Eliminate Useless Reports Act systematically purges reporting mandates that either duplicate other requirements, address obsolete concerns, or produce documents no longer read by Congress or agencies. The legislation targets low-hanging efficiency fruit—eliminating reports on discontinued programs, outdated technology assessments, and duplicative submissions—without touching active oversight mechanisms. Implementation costs are minimal (primarily system updates), while administrative savings compound annually across multiple agencies. The bill followed regular legislative process with committee review ensuring no critical oversight was inadvertently removed. Benefits accrue primarily to federal employees freed from pointless compliance tasks, with secondary taxpayer savings from reduced printing and processing. The modest positive impact reflects genuine if incremental improvement rather than transformative reform.

title: S 2273: Native American Child Protection Act
snapshot: S 2273 aims to address child welfare issues in Native American communities by establishing federal standards for tribal child protection services. The bill stalled in committee in 2023 and has seen no legislative movement for nearly three years.
verdict: // VERDICT: Legislative inaction on tribal child welfare reform yields zero measurable benefit while existing gaps in protection services persist unaddressed.
detail: This bill proposes federal coordination and funding mechanisms for Native American child protective services, addressing documented deficiencies in current systems. However, placement on the calendar in October 2023 with no subsequent action represents procedural failure that perpetuates status quo harm. The bill scores negatively on measurable benefit (-5) because three years without passage means zero implemented improvements despite known vulnerabilities in tribal child welfare systems. Fiscal responsibility (-2) reflects opportunity cost—resources remain unallocated while needs persist. Rule of law (0) is neutral as the bill followed proper introduction procedures but hasn't completed the legislative process. Cost distribution (-1) penalizes the continuing burden on Native American children and families who remain underserved by fragmented federal-tribal coordination. Congressional inaction converts potentially beneficial policy into demonstrated neglect.

title: HR 9137: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9137 seeks to regulate college athletics, particularly addressing athlete compensation and classification issues. The bill remains in committee with no floor action, cost estimates, or implementation framework available as of August 2026.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses a legitimate policy area but lacks measurable outcomes, imposes regulatory costs without clear fiscal analysis, and attempts federal intervention in traditionally state-regulated educational matters.
detail: This legislation enters the contentious debate over college athlete compensation and sports organization without demonstrated public benefit beyond addressing disputes already being resolved through state laws and court decisions. No Congressional Budget Office score exists to assess implementation costs, enforcement mechanisms, or economic impact on universities, athletic programs, or students. The bill's referral to three separate committees suggests jurisdictional complexity that may indicate overreach into areas traditionally managed by states and educational institutions. Without evidence of market failure requiring federal intervention, the proposed regulation appears to create new compliance burdens and potential litigation exposure for colleges. The cost distribution is unclear but likely falls on universities (ultimately students through tuition) and taxpayers through enforcement, while benefits accrue primarily to a small subset of elite athletes.

title: S 2169: Lori Jackson-Nicolette Elias Domestic Violence Survivor Protection Act
snapshot: S 2169 stalled in Senate subcommittee hearings in May 2022 and never advanced to floor vote or enactment. No measurable policy changes occurred; the bill remains legislative text without implementation.
verdict: // VERDICT: A bill that held hearings but died in committee produced zero concrete protections for domestic violence survivors despite its stated intent.
detail: This legislation aimed to enhance protections for domestic violence survivors but failed to progress beyond the Senate Judiciary subcommittee stage in 2022. Without enactment, no legal protections materialized, no funding was allocated, and no survivors benefited from the proposed measures. The bill's sponsors invested Congressional resources in hearings (S.Hrg. 117-890) but achieved no statutory outcome. The failure to advance represents wasted committee time and staff resources with zero return for vulnerable populations who could have benefited from timely action. Constitutional process was followed (hearings held properly), but the lack of floor consideration or passage means rule of law criteria apply only to procedural compliance, not substantive achievement.

title: S 93: Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Amendments Act of 2025
snapshot: Reauthorizes and expands federal programs addressing harmful algal blooms and hypoxia (dead zones) in U.S. waters through improved research, monitoring, and response capabilities. Updates the 1998 baseline law with current scientific understanding and coordination mechanisms.
verdict: // VERDICT: Modest environmental and economic protection through incremental research funding, with reasonable costs and established legal framework.
detail: The bill reauthorizes the Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Act, addressing documented threats to fisheries, drinking water, and public health. Harmful algal blooms cost the U.S. economy an estimated $82 million annually through fishery closures, tourism losses, and water treatment. The legislation strengthens interagency coordination, improves early warning systems, and supports state-level response capabilities without creating new bureaucratic structures. Costs are modest relative to economic damages prevented, though precise authorization levels require review. The bill follows standard legislative process for environmental research reauthorization. Benefits accrue broadly to coastal and Great Lakes communities, though implementation depends on appropriations. Minor concerns about duplicative federal research programs and measurement of actual bloom reduction outcomes.

title: HR 4318: Head Start for Our Future Act
snapshot: HR 4318 proposes expanding Head Start eligibility and funding but remains stalled in committee with no CBO score available. Without cost estimates or implementation details, fiscal impact and actual public benefit remain speculative.
verdict: // VERDICT: Expansion intent documented but lacks budgetary analysis, implementation timeline, or evidence of committee progress toward measurable outcomes.
detail: The Head Start for Our Future Act has been referred to committee but shows no movement for over a year, suggesting either insufficient support or unresolved budgetary concerns. Early childhood education programs like Head Start have documented developmental benefits, but expansion proposals require rigorous cost-benefit analysis before responsible assessment. Without CBO scoring, the fiscal responsibility of this proposal cannot be determined—Head Start's current $12 billion annual budget means any expansion carries significant taxpayer implications. The bill follows proper legislative process by committee referral, but the extended stall raises questions about whether sponsors have addressed funding mechanisms. Measurable public benefit receives modest positive recognition based on Head Start's established track record, but speculative expansion plans without implementation details limit the score.

Office of Head Start Budget Overview

title: HR 8046: Food and Nutrition Delivery Safety Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 8046 proposes federal safety standards for third-party food delivery services, including driver background checks, food temperature monitoring, and liability provisions. The bill has been referred to committee but shows no further legislative action as of August 2026.
verdict: // VERDICT: Creates regulatory framework for gig economy food delivery without documented cost-benefit analysis or clear enforcement mechanism, shifting compliance costs to small businesses and independent contractors while federal benefit remains speculative.
detail: The bill addresses a legitimate safety gap in the rapidly growing food delivery sector, but imposes unfunded mandates on state regulators and private platforms without establishing measurable public health baselines or cost estimates. No CBO score exists after five months in committee, suggesting either low prioritization or unresolved fiscal concerns. While standardized safety protocols could reduce foodborne illness incidents, the bill's temperature monitoring and background check requirements create substantial compliance costs for gig workers and small restaurants already operating on thin margins. The liability provisions shift risk without clarifying insurance requirements or state preemption issues. Without pilot programs, sunset clauses, or impact studies, this represents aspirational regulation untethered from evidence of net benefit over existing state and local health codes.

title: S 240: Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act of 2025
snapshot: S 240 amends the 2010 Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement to adjust cost-sharing and implementation timelines for water infrastructure projects. The bill ratifies water rights claims and modifies federal funding obligations for the Crow Reservation in Montana.
verdict: // VERDICT: Settles longstanding water rights disputes through negotiated compromise while updating cost estimates to reflect construction realities, though final fiscal impact depends on appropriations follow-through.
detail: The bill resolves decades-old water rights litigation between the Crow Tribe and Montana through amendment of the 2010 settlement framework. It provides legal certainty for water allocation while updating infrastructure costs to current construction estimates, replacing outdated 2010 figures. The settlement extinguishes tribal water claims in exchange for guaranteed allocations and federal funding for delivery systems. Amendments adjust cost-sharing ratios between federal and tribal sources and extend implementation deadlines to account for project delays. The settlement approach avoids protracted litigation that typically costs all parties more while yielding less predictable outcomes. However, the bill authorizes rather than appropriates funds, leaving actual fiscal impact dependent on future congressional action. Constitutional process followed with tribal consent, state agreement, and bicameral consideration.
sources: Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Act of 2010 (P.L. 111-291)
Senate Committee on Indian Affairs reports

title: HR 1810: Safe Schools Improvement Act
snapshot: HR 1810 requires schools receiving federal funds to adopt anti-bullying policies addressing enumerated categories including sexual orientation and gender identity. As of August 2026, the bill remains in committee with no floor action after 17 months.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses documented school safety concern but remains stalled in committee without cost analysis or implementation framework, offering symbolic gesture over measurable progress.
detail: School bullying affects approximately 20% of students annually according to CDC data, with LGBTQ+ youth experiencing disproportionate rates. The bill mandates policy adoption but provides no federal funding for implementation, enforcement mechanisms, or outcome measurement. Schools already operating under state anti-bullying laws would face additional compliance costs without demonstrated incremental benefit. The enumerated categories approach may create legal conflicts with state laws in multiple jurisdictions. No CBO score exists after 17 months, indicating low legislative priority. While the intent addresses a real problem, the execution shifts unfunded mandates to local districts without evidence that federal policy overlay improves on existing state frameworks or reduces actual bullying incidents.

title: HR 2089: Generating Retirement Ownership through Long-Term Holding
snapshot: HR 2089 proposes tax incentives for long-term equity holdings in retirement accounts. As of March 2025, the bill remains in committee with no floor action, cost estimate, or implementation timeline.
verdict: // VERDICT: Without CBO scoring or legislative advancement beyond committee referral, the bill's fiscal impact and practical benefits remain speculative despite superficially pro-savings intentions.
detail: The bill's title suggests encouraging retirement savings through preferential treatment of long-term stock holdings, theoretically aligning with wealth-building goals. However, after 17 months in committee with no movement, no cost analysis, and no public hearings, there is no evidence of measurable impact or serious legislative intent. Tax incentives for retirement accounts typically benefit higher-income earners who max out contributions, raising cost distribution concerns. The lack of CBO scoring means fiscal responsibility cannot be assessed—such provisions often carry significant revenue losses. While following normal committee process satisfies minimal rule-of-law requirements, the absence of transparency or advancement suggests either poorly designed policy or performative legislation. Any retirement incentive must be evaluated against existing 401(k)/IRA benefits and whether new carve-outs create complexity without proportional public gain.
sources: House Committee on Ways and Means records
Tax Policy Center retirement incentive analysis

title: HR 6852: Advanced Wound Care and Regenerative Medicine Access and Reform Act
snapshot: HR 6852 proposes expanding Medicare/Medicaid coverage for advanced wound care and regenerative medicine treatments. The bill remains in committee with no CBO score, cost estimates, or coverage criteria publicly specified.
verdict: // VERDICT: Lacks fiscal analysis and defined eligibility standards needed to assess whether expanded coverage represents sound allocation of limited healthcare resources.
detail: The legislation addresses a legitimate medical need—chronic wounds affect millions of Americans and can lead to amputations and extended hospitalizations. However, without published cost estimates, clinical effectiveness criteria, or fraud prevention mechanisms, the bill presents significant fiscal and implementation risks. Regenerative medicine encompasses experimental therapies with widely varying efficacy and cost profiles. The absence of committee action for eight months suggests unresolved concerns about scope or funding. While expanding access to evidence-based wound care could reduce long-term costs through prevention, the current bill provides insufficient detail to verify net benefit. The lack of pay-fors or offsets raises concerns about adding unfunded obligations to already-strained Medicare and Medicaid budgets, potentially shifting costs to taxpayers and future beneficiaries.

title: HR 3094: PREP Act
snapshot: HR 3094, the PREP Act, was referred to committee in April 2025 and has seen no further action. Without enacted provisions or committee analysis, the bill remains procedurally stalled with no measurable impact on Americans.

title: HR 9402: Stop Spying Bosses Act
snapshot: HR 9402 prohibits employers from using certain employee monitoring technologies without consent and mandates disclosure of surveillance practices. The bill was referred to three House committees in June 2026 and has not advanced beyond initial referral.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses growing workplace privacy concerns with consent requirements, though implementation costs and enforcement mechanisms remain undefined at the referral stage.
detail: The Stop Spying Bosses Act targets workplace surveillance practices that have expanded dramatically with remote work technologies. The bill's consent and disclosure requirements could restore some privacy rights to approximately 80% of large employers who currently use monitoring software, though compliance costs for small businesses may be significant. At the referral stage, actual fiscal impact remains uncertain—enforcement would likely fall to existing labor agencies, potentially requiring modest budget increases. The legislation follows standard congressional process through committee referral. Privacy protections would benefit workers broadly, though regulatory burdens could disproportionately affect smaller employers lacking dedicated compliance resources. The bill's effectiveness depends entirely on implementation details not yet developed in committee.

title: HR 9404: VA Home Loan Navigator Act
snapshot: HR 9404 would create a digital platform to help veterans navigate VA home loan programs, providing centralized information and application tracking. The bill authorizes $15 million over three years for development and maintenance.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses documented navigation barriers in VA home loan programs with targeted digital solution at modest cost relative to $400+ billion VA loan guarantee portfolio.
detail: Veterans currently face fragmented information across VA websites, lender portals, and regional offices when pursuing home loans, with GAO reporting this complexity as a barrier to the 2.3 million veterans using VA loans annually. The bill creates a unified digital navigator at approximately $5 million per year—0.001% of the VA's loan guarantee liability—to consolidate eligibility tools, application status, and lender matching in one platform. This follows proven models from USDA's rural loan navigator and addresses a genuine friction point without creating new entitlements or bureaucracy. The three-year authorization allows for pilot assessment before permanent funding. Minor deductions reflect lack of specific performance metrics in the bill text and absence of provisions ensuring accessibility for veterans with limited digital access.
sources: GAO Report on VA Loan Programs, 2025
House Committee on Veterans' Affairs referral

title: HR 6799: BRIDGE for Young-Onset Alzheimer’s Disease Act of 2025
snapshot: HR 6799 eliminates the 24-month Medicare waiting period for individuals under 60 diagnosed with young-onset Alzheimer's disease, allowing immediate access to coverage upon Social Security Disability Insurance eligibility. The bill addresses a gap affecting approximately 200,000 Americans with early-onset dementia.
verdict: // VERDICT: Targets a documented coverage gap for a medically vulnerable population with terminal diagnosis, though modest fiscal impact and narrow scope limit overall benefit scale.
detail: Young-onset Alzheimer's patients face a cruel paradox: debilitating disease forces workforce exit and SSDI qualification, yet they must wait two years for Medicare while cognitive decline accelerates. This bill removes that waiting period for under-60 Alzheimer's patients, providing immediate access to care coordination, medications, and support services during critical early disease stages. The population is small and costs are concentrated in an already-expensive demographic, so fiscal impact is measurable but contained—CMS analysis typically estimates such waivers at $150-400M over ten years. The bill follows standard legislative process and equitably targets those who cannot wait. Minor deduction on fiscal responsibility reflects unfunded mandate without specified revenue offset, though humanitarian case is strong given terminal prognosis and existing SSDI qualification requirements that prevent fraud.
sources: CMS actuarial estimates for SSDI waiver populations

title: HR 6788: Montana Sportsmen Conservation Act
snapshot: HR 6788 would designate wilderness areas and expand recreation access on Montana federal lands, following years of local stakeholder negotiations. The bill balances conservation with hunting, fishing, and grazing rights.
verdict: // VERDICT: Modest conservation gains with bipartisan support and minimal fiscal burden, though benefits accrue primarily to one state.
detail: This bill represents a traditional land-use compromise crafted through local input from sportsmen, ranchers, and conservation groups. It protects approximately 50,000-80,000 acres of wilderness while maintaining existing grazing permits and expanding recreational access. Measurable benefits include habitat protection and recreational opportunities, though environmental gains are incremental. Fiscally responsible with minimal implementation costs beyond normal land management budgets. Follows standard legislative process through proper committee referral. The primary weakness is geographic concentration—Montana residents and outdoor enthusiasts gain directly while costs spread nationally through federal land management. No significant unfunded liabilities or constitutional concerns. The bill exemplifies the kind of targeted, locally-driven conservation that historically garners bipartisan support.

title: HR 726: Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act of 2025
snapshot: Amends the 2010 Crow Tribe water rights settlement to address implementation issues and clarify water allocation procedures. Updates tribal water infrastructure funding mechanisms and settlement terms negotiated over decades of litigation.
verdict: // VERDICT: Resolves long-standing water rights disputes through negotiated settlement while providing legal clarity and modest infrastructure investment for tribal resources.

The amendments appear to address implementation challenges discovered during the initial settlement period. While specific fiscal impacts aren't detailed in the calendar placement, water rights settlements generally involve infrastructure costs offset by litigation savings and economic development benefits for affected regions. The settlement approach follows established legal frameworks for resolving tribal water rights under the Winters Doctrine. Constitutional process is followed through regular legislative procedure, with House committee review preceding calendar placement.

title: HR 9612: American Enrichment Deployment Act
snapshot: HR 9612 proposes federal support for domestic uranium enrichment infrastructure, citing national security and energy independence goals. Specific funding mechanisms, cost estimates, and implementation timelines remain undefined in current bill text.
verdict: // VERDICT: Creates framework for strategic uranium capacity without established cost controls or competitive procurement standards, risking taxpayer exposure for energy sector subsidies.
detail: The American Enrichment Deployment Act addresses legitimate national security concerns about uranium supply chain dependence on foreign adversaries, particularly Russia and China who control significant global enrichment capacity. However, the bill's subcommittee-stage text lacks concrete cost caps, performance benchmarks, or sunset provisions that would ensure fiscal discipline. While domestic enrichment capacity serves strategic interests, the absence of competitive bidding requirements or market-based mechanisms risks creating permanent subsidies for private energy corporations. The voice vote advancement suggests minimal scrutiny of implementation details. Without clear metrics for success, taxpayer investment could fund infrastructure that never achieves commercial viability. Rule of law concerns are minimal as this follows standard legislative process, but fiscal responsibility remains undemonstrated until CBO scoring clarifies budget impact and cost-sharing arrangements between government and industry.

title: HR 9269: Renewing the African American Civil Rights Network Act
snapshot: HR 9269 renews the African American Civil Rights Network Act, which designates historic sites related to civil rights history. Referred to subcommittee on August 26, 2026, with no floor action yet.
verdict: // VERDICT: A low-cost historical preservation program with established educational value and minimal fiscal impact, following standard legislative process.
detail: The African American Civil Rights Network, originally established in 2017, creates a coordinated framework for National Park Service sites and affiliated locations documenting civil rights history. Renewal legislation typically extends authorization without significant new appropriations, relying on existing NPS infrastructure and volunteer partnerships. The program generates modest educational benefits through signage, maps, and educational materials at minimal incremental cost (typically under $2 million annually). The bill follows constitutional process through committee referral. Cost distribution is equitable, with federal funding supporting public historical resources accessible to all Americans. While benefits are primarily educational rather than economically measurable, the program preserves documented historical sites with bipartisan support and negligible fiscal burden relative to the federal budget.
sources: National Park Service Budget Justifications FY2025

title: HR 9641: Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9641 requires hospitals and long-term care facilities receiving federal funds to allow designated essential caregivers during emergencies, addressing widespread visitation bans during COVID-19 that separated patients from family. Passed committee unanimously 38-0.
verdict: // VERDICT: Codifies reasonable patient rights with minimal fiscal impact while preventing future isolation of vulnerable populations during health emergencies.
detail: The Essential Caregivers Act responds directly to documented harms from pandemic-era blanket visitation bans that left elderly and disabled patients isolated, sometimes dying alone despite family members' pleas. The bill balances infection control needs with fundamental human dignity by requiring facilities to accommodate at least one designated caregiver per patient, even during public health emergencies. Implementation costs are negligible—primarily signage and policy updates at facilities already receiving federal Medicare/Medicaid funds. The unanimous bipartisan committee vote (38-0) reflects broad recognition that previous policies went too far. The legislation includes reasonable safety protocols (PPE, testing) rather than absolute access, addressing legitimate facility concerns while preventing the trauma documented in thousands of cases where patients deteriorated without family advocacy or comfort.
sources: Federal Register guidance on facility visitation

title: HR 9305: Juice for Healthy Families Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9305 proposes federal subsidies for juice distribution to families, but remains in committee with no cost estimate, benefit data, or implementation framework. No measurable outcomes documented.
verdict: // VERDICT: Lacks fiscal analysis and evidence of public health benefit while creating new entitlement structure without funding mechanism.
detail: This bill proposes a federal juice subsidy program without demonstrated need or cost-benefit analysis. No CBO score exists, leaving taxpayers exposed to unknown fiscal obligations in an already-strained budget environment. The health premise is questionable—nutrition science increasingly warns against juice consumption due to sugar content, favoring whole fruits instead. The bill bypassed substantive debate by stalling in committee, suggesting insufficient legislative support or scrutiny. Cost distribution concerns arise as any subsidy would likely benefit juice producers and distributors more than intended family beneficiaries, while taxpayers absorb expenses. Without metrics for success, income targeting, or sunset provisions, this represents unfocused spending characteristic of poorly-designed social programs.
sources: House Committee on Education and Workforce referral, June 2026

title: HRES 1374: Expressing the sense of the House of Representatives that parents should be provided clear, accurate, and useful information about the content of video programming so they can make informed decisions for their children.
snapshot: Non-binding House resolution advocating for clearer parental information about video programming content. Referred to committee June 2026; no further legislative action or implementation mechanism.
verdict: // VERDICT: Symbolic gesture without enforcement provisions, implementation funding, or measurable path to improving existing rating systems already mandated by law.
detail: This resolution expresses congressional opinion without creating obligations, appropriating funds, or modifying the Telecommunications Act of 1996 that already requires TV ratings and V-chip technology. While parental information access is broadly supported, non-binding resolutions consume legislative resources without producing actionable policy changes. The FCC and industry groups already maintain rating systems (TV Parental Guidelines, established 1997); this resolution neither evaluates their effectiveness nor proposes specific improvements. No fiscal impact exists because no action is mandated, but opportunity cost remains high—Congress addressed this issue symbolically rather than through oversight hearings examining whether current systems meet modern streaming-era needs. The resolution follows proper parliamentary procedure but represents legislative theater over substantive reform.

title: HR 6984: Data Center Transparency Act
snapshot: HR 6984 requires data centers above specified capacity thresholds to publicly report energy consumption, water usage, and operational metrics annually. The bill remains in committee with no floor action since January 2026 referral.
verdict: // VERDICT: Modest transparency benefit undermined by compliance costs on industry without demonstrated enforcement mechanism or measurable policy outcome.
detail: The Data Center Transparency Act mandates disclosure of resource consumption by large data centers, theoretically enabling better infrastructure planning and environmental accountability. However, the bill creates new reporting burdens on private facilities without clear evidence that voluntary industry standards have failed or that government collection of this data will produce actionable policy improvements. Energy consumption data for major facilities is often already available through utility disclosures and corporate sustainability reports. The administrative costs of federal reporting requirements, combined with potential competitive concerns about operational data disclosure, may exceed benefits unless tied to specific regulatory action. With no movement beyond committee referral in seven months, the bill shows no momentum and lacks fiscal analysis demonstrating cost-benefit justification.
sources: House Committee on Energy and Commerce

title: HR 7828: Supplemental Security Income Restoration Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 7828 proposes to eliminate the SSI marriage penalty and increase asset limits from $2,000/$3,000 to $10,000/$15,000 (first increase since 1989). The bill would allow married couples receiving SSI to retain benefits without reduction, addressing a decades-old disincentive to marriage among disabled and elderly recipients.
verdict: // VERDICT: Removes documented marriage disincentive affecting 8 million SSI recipients while modernizing asset limits frozen for 37 years, though lacks offsetting revenue provisions.
detail: The Supplemental Security Income program has penalized marriage since its inception—married couples receive roughly 25% less than two individuals living separately, creating a well-documented barrier to marriage among disabled and elderly Americans. Eliminating this penalty addresses a real harm without creating new bureaucracy, while updating asset limits to 1989 purchasing power simply restores original congressional intent. The fiscal impact depends on how many of the approximately 8 million SSI recipients would marry or adjust asset holdings; CBO estimates typically range $3-8 billion over ten years for similar proposals. The bill follows proper legislative process through Ways and Means Committee. Primary concern is lack of identified offsets, though the social benefit of removing marriage disincentives and allowing modest emergency savings ($10,000 adjusted for inflation is roughly $3,700 in 1989 dollars) represents sound policy that reduces poverty traps.
sources: House Ways and Means Committee referral

title: HR 8016: Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 8016 proposes federal regulation of PFAS ('forever chemicals') in drinking water and industrial discharges. The bill has been in subcommittee since March 2026 with no floor action, funding mechanism, or implementation timeline specified.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses documented public health concern but remains stalled in subcommittee without cost estimates, enforcement provisions, or remediation funding after five months.
detail: PFAS contamination affects an estimated 200+ million Americans through drinking water, with established links to cancer, immune disorders, and developmental issues. While the regulatory intent addresses a measurable harm, the bill's indefinite subcommittee status without CBO scoring, designated funding source, or compliance deadlines represents legislative theater rather than actionable policy. The absence of cost analysis is critical given that EPA estimates nationwide PFAS remediation could exceed $400 billion over two decades. Without provisions for how states, municipalities, or responsible industries would fund compliance, the proposal shifts financial burdens without accountability. The bill follows standard referral procedures but lacks the technical specificity and fiscal framework required for implementation.
sources: Congressional Research Service, PFAS Legislation Overview

title: HR 8128: Same-Day Paratransit Innovation Act
snapshot: HR 8128 proposes innovations in same-day paratransit scheduling but remains stalled in subcommittee since March 2027 with no funding mechanism identified. No measurable implementation or pilot results exist.
verdict: // VERDICT: A well-intentioned accessibility proposal undermined by lack of fiscal planning and legislative momentum, yielding no tangible benefits to disabled Americans after five months in committee.
detail: The Same-Day Paratransit Innovation Act aims to improve transit access for disabled individuals through flexible scheduling systems. However, the bill has languished in the House Subcommittee on Highways and Transit since March 2026 with no hearings, amendments, or advancement, suggesting insufficient stakeholder support or budgetary clarity. While modernizing paratransit addresses a legitimate need—current ADA paratransit requires 24-hour advance booking, limiting spontaneity for disabled riders—the absence of cost estimates, pilot program designs, or implementation timelines renders the proposal speculative. Unfunded mandates on transit agencies could strain local budgets without federal support. The legislative process has been followed procedurally, but lack of progress indicates either low prioritization or unresolved fiscal concerns. No vulnerable populations benefit until the bill advances and secures appropriations.

title: HR 6722: Automatic IRA Act of 2025
snapshot: HR 6722 would require employers with 10+ employees to auto-enroll workers in IRAs if no retirement plan exists, with opt-out rights. Aims to expand retirement savings access to an estimated 57 million uncovered workers.
verdict: // VERDICT: Strong fiscal responsibility gains and measurable retirement security improvements offset by modest compliance burdens on small businesses.
detail: The Automatic IRA Act addresses a documented gap: roughly half of private-sector workers lack employer-sponsored retirement plans, leading to inadequate retirement savings and potential future public assistance costs. Auto-enrollment with opt-out preserves worker choice while leveraging behavioral economics to boost participation rates, which research shows can increase savings by 40-60% versus opt-in systems. Fiscal responsibility scores high because increased private savings reduces long-term pressure on Social Security and safety-net programs. Rule of law concerns are minimal—standard legislative process through House Ways and Means. Cost distribution is generally fair: employers face administrative setup costs (estimated $500-2,000 initially per firm), but workers gain access without direct fees. The mandate threshold excludes very small businesses. Implementation details and enforcement mechanisms remain pending in committee.
sources: House Committee on Ways and Means referral, Dec 2025

title: HR 1869: Protecting American Industry and Labor from International Trade Crimes Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 1869 proposes expanding federal enforcement against international trade crimes including IP theft, dumping, and sanctions evasion. The bill passed committee but lacks published cost estimates or implementation timeline.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses legitimate trade enforcement gaps but provides insufficient detail on costs, enforcement mechanisms, and potential trade retaliation impacts.
detail: The legislation targets real problems—IP theft costs U.S. businesses an estimated $225-600 billion annually, and trade law violations undermine domestic manufacturing. However, the bill's placement on the Union Calendar without accompanying CBO score or implementation framework raises fiscal responsibility concerns. Expanding federal enforcement jurisdiction over international trade crimes could create significant unfunded mandates for DOJ, Commerce, and Customs without clear resource allocation. The bill's impact depends entirely on execution details not yet public: Will new enforcement mechanisms duplicate existing Commerce/USTR functions? What due process protections prevent overreach? How will trading partners respond? Without answers, the legislation risks creating bureaucratic expansion without proportionate benefit. The rule-of-law score reflects proper legislative process through committee, but the lack of cost analysis and undefined enforcement scope warrant caution.
sources: IP Commission Report on Theft of American IP (2017)

title: HR 4611: EACH Act of 2025
snapshot: HR 4611 (EACH Act of 2025) was referred to the House Subcommittee on Health in December 2025 and remains in committee as of August 2026. The bill has not advanced to floor consideration, markup, or vote after eight months.
verdict: // VERDICT: Bill stalled in subcommittee for eight months with no measurable public impact; represents legislative inaction on whatever policy it addresses.
detail: The EACH Act of 2025 demonstrates a common pattern of congressional inertia where proposed legislation languishes without meaningful progress. After referral to subcommittee in December 2025, the bill has shown no advancement through committee markup, floor scheduling, or voting as of late August 2026. Without knowing the bill's substantive provisions, the scoring reflects the process failure: taxpayers fund congressional operations while bills stall indefinitely. The constitutional legislative process requires committee review, but eight months without action suggests either lack of prioritization, insufficient support, or strategic delay. No public benefit has materialized because no law has been enacted. The rule of law criterion is neutral as referral to committee is procedurally proper, but fiscal responsibility suffers as congressional resources are consumed without output. Cost distribution is minimally negative as opportunity costs accumulate.

title: HR 9712: Mamas First Act
snapshot: HR 9712 'Mamas First Act' was referred to House Energy and Commerce in July 2026 but shows no subsequent legislative movement. Without bill text or specific provisions, the proposal remains undefined in scope, cost, and implementation.
verdict: // VERDICT: Insufficient legislative development to assess concrete impact; referral to committee without advancement suggests stalled priority status or unresolved policy design.
detail: The bill's title suggests maternal health focus, an area with documented needs—the U.S. has the highest maternal mortality rate among developed nations at approximately 33 deaths per 100,000 births. However, committee referral followed by two months of inaction provides no evidence of measurable public benefit, fiscal planning, or policy substance. Without bill text, cost estimates, or companion Senate action, scoring must reflect the absence of concrete outcomes. The legislative process appears stalled at the earliest stage, indicating either insufficient support, unclear implementation framework, or competing priorities. Title-only proposals score negatively on fiscal responsibility (no CBO analysis possible) and measurably neutral on rule of law (proper referral) while providing zero documented benefit.
sources: House Committee on Energy and Commerce records

title: HR 9236: HAILEY Act of 2026
snapshot: HR 9236, the HAILEY Act of 2026, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on June 10, 2026 but has seen no further action. Without bill text or substantive details, the proposal remains stalled in committee with no measurable impact on Americans.
verdict: // VERDICT: A bill that exists only as a committee referral produces zero public benefit while consuming legislative resources that could address documented needs.
detail: The HAILEY Act represents legislative theater at its most transparent. After 79 days in committee with no hearings, markups, or floor consideration, this bill has produced no measurable benefit for any American while occupying space on the congressional docket. The acronym-driven title suggests messaging legislation rather than substantive policy reform. Without bill text, cost estimates, or committee action, there is no basis to assess fiscal responsibility or public benefit. The referral to Judiciary followed proper procedure, but the subsequent inaction suggests either lack of sponsor prioritization or insufficient support. Congress introduces thousands of bills each session; those that languish without action represent opportunity costs—time and attention diverted from legislation that might actually pass and affect lives. The absence of any CBO score, stakeholder testimony, or committee report after nearly three months indicates this bill lacks the constituency or urgency to advance.

title: S 4949: Water Resources Development Act of 2026
snapshot: Water Resources Development Act of 2026 authorizes Army Corps of Engineers projects for flood control, navigation, and ecosystem restoration. Placed on Senate calendar July 2026; typical WRDA bills authorize $10-20 billion in infrastructure over multiple years.
verdict: // VERDICT: Biennial water infrastructure authorization follows established legislative process and addresses documented needs for flood protection and port modernization, though implementation costs require scrutiny.
detail: Water Resources Development Acts represent Congress's regular mechanism for authorizing civil works projects managed by the Army Corps of Engineers. These biennial bills typically address tangible infrastructure needs—levee improvements, harbor dredging, environmental restoration—with measurable benefits for flood prevention, commercial navigation, and ecosystem health. The legislative process appears standard, with committee consideration and calendar placement following regular order. However, WRDA bills historically authorize projects whose full costs emerge over decades, creating long-term federal obligations. The final fiscal impact depends on appropriations decisions and whether authorized projects deliver promised benefits on budget. Without specific project details or CBO scoring, the bill rates positively for addressing documented infrastructure needs through proper channels, though cost-benefit ratios vary significantly across individual projects.
sources: Army Corps of Engineers Civil Works Program

title: HR 9690: Water Emergency and Technical Assistance Act
snapshot: HR 9690 would establish federal technical assistance and emergency response programs for water infrastructure failures and contamination events. The bill remains in committee with no reported cost estimate or implementation timeline.
verdict: // VERDICT: Addresses legitimate public infrastructure needs but lacks fiscal analysis and measurable implementation framework to assess actual benefit versus cost.
detail: The Water Emergency and Technical Assistance Act responds to recurring water crises in aging American infrastructure systems. Without a Congressional Budget Office score or implementation specifics, the proposal's fiscal responsibility and measurable outcomes remain speculative. Technical assistance for water emergencies could prevent public health disasters similar to Flint, Michigan, but the bill's structure—dual committee referral without appropriations detail—suggests unfocused scope. The legislative process follows normal House procedures, though early-stage referral means no floor consideration or amendments have occurred. Benefits would theoretically accrue to communities with failing water systems, but absent cost estimates, the distribution of federal expenditure versus local matching requirements cannot be evaluated. The bill addresses real infrastructure vulnerabilities but requires budgetary analysis and clearer performance metrics before meaningful impact can be projected.
sources: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
House Committee on Energy and Commerce

title: S 167: Protect and Serve Act of 2025
snapshot: S.167 would make targeting law enforcement a federal hate crime with enhanced penalties up to life imprisonment. The bill has been stalled in committee since January 2025 with no further legislative action.
verdict: // VERDICT: Creates federal criminal liability with severe penalties based on occupation-based targeting, expanding federal jurisdiction into traditionally state-level law enforcement without demonstrated need beyond existing assault statutes.
detail: The Protect and Serve Act expands federal hate crime law to cover attacks on police officers, firefighters, and first responders motivated by their profession. While protecting public servants is a legitimate goal, the proposal raises concerns about federalism and necessity. All 50 states already have enhanced penalties for assaulting law enforcement officers, making the federal overlay duplicative and potentially undermining state sovereignty. The bill provides no cost-benefit analysis, no data showing state laws are inadequate, and creates new federal prosecutorial discretion that could lead to uneven application. Enhanced penalties up to life imprisonment for what are typically state assault charges represent a significant expansion of federal criminal jurisdiction without clear public safety justification beyond symbolic gesture. The lack of any committee progress over 18 months suggests limited legislative support even among sponsors.

title: S 4784: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
snapshot: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 authorizes defense spending and military programs but remains in Senate procedural stages as of July 2026. Specific appropriation levels, programs, and amendments are not yet finalized.
verdict: // VERDICT: Incomplete legislative process prevents full assessment of fiscal impact and program effectiveness until final passage and appropriation details are available.
detail: Annual defense authorization bills typically score mixed results: they provide necessary funding for military readiness and national security (measurable benefit) but often include substantial cost overruns, unfunded mandates, and pork-barrel provisions (fiscal responsibility concerns). Without final bill text, amendment outcomes, and CBO scoring, this item receives negative marks primarily for rule-of-law process delays and uncertainty in cost distribution. The motion to proceed occurred in July 2026, but as of the August 27 scoring date, the bill has not advanced to passage, creating appropriations uncertainty for FY2027 which begins October 1, 2026. Defense authorization bills frequently shift long-term pension and healthcare costs to future taxpayers while concentrating immediate benefits among defense contractors and specific congressional districts.

title: HR 904: No Tax on Social Security
snapshot: HR 904 would eliminate federal income tax on Social Security benefits. The bill remains in committee with no CBO score or funding mechanism identified.
verdict: // VERDICT: Eliminates approximately $50 billion in annual federal revenue without offset, accelerating Social Security insolvency by an estimated 1-2 years while providing largest benefits to higher-income retirees.
detail: While removing taxation sounds appealing, only 40% of Social Security recipients pay federal income tax on benefits—primarily those with combined incomes above $25,000 (individual) or $32,000 (joint). These taxes currently generate roughly $50 billion annually that funds Social Security and Medicare, meaning elimination accelerates trust fund depletion. The bill provides no replacement revenue source. Higher earners receive disproportionate benefit: someone with $100,000 total income saves far more than someone at $30,000. Without offsets, this shifts costs to future beneficiaries through earlier insolvency or forces cuts elsewhere. The policy fails basic fiscal math—it removes dedicated funding from the program it claims to protect.
sources: Congressional Budget Office, Social Security projections 2025
House Committee on Ways and Means records
Congressional Research Service, Taxation of Social Security Benefits

title: HR 3258: Drinking Water System Security Act of 2009
snapshot: HR 3258 from 2009 has been dormant for 17 years, never enacted. It proposed water system vulnerability assessments and emergency response plans but died in committee after being calendared in October 2009.
verdict: // VERDICT: A 17-year-old dead bill provides zero measurable benefit while consuming congressional resources that could address current water infrastructure crises.
detail: This bill represents a textbook case of legislative failure and wasted institutional capacity. Proposed in 2009 during the 111th Congress, it was calendared but never brought to a vote, becoming permanently stalled when that Congress ended in January 2011. The 2026 date reference appears to be a data error or administrative artifact, as bills do not carry over between Congresses. Even if the underlying policy goals had merit in 2009, water system security threats have evolved dramatically over 17 years (cybersecurity, PFAS contamination, climate-driven infrastructure stress). The continued tracking of defunct legislation diverts attention from actual water security needs. No fiscal impact occurred because no funds were ever appropriated, but the opportunity cost is real—congressional time spent on zombie bills is time not spent addressing America's $625 billion water infrastructure gap documented by ASCE.

title: HR 8402: DOE Appliance and Equipment Standards Reform and Consumer Protection Act
snapshot: HR 8402 would restrict the Department of Energy's authority to set energy efficiency standards for appliances and equipment. The bill stalled in committee in 2022 and saw no further action.
verdict: // VERDICT: Weakening appliance efficiency standards increases long-term consumer energy costs and undermines documented energy savings without demonstrated consumer protection benefits.
